_instructions.purpose: A worked example, used to build the sample PDFs in the release. The person is invented. Copy resume_data.template.json to resume_data.json for your own, and this file will step aside.
_instructions.why_it_reads_this_way: Every bullet leads with an outcome and carries a number. Nothing here says 'responsible for'. That is the whole difference between a resume that is read and one that is skimmed.

resume.summary: Machine learning engineer with five years building retrieval and inference systems in production. Strongest on the unglamorous half: evaluation, latency and cost.

bullets: Rebuilt the retrieval layer behind a 40M document assistant, cutting median answer latency from 2.4s to 610ms by replacing per query re-ranking with a cached two stage retriever.
Cut inference spend 38% year on year, roughly 1.2M USD, by routing 71% of traffic to a distilled 3B model and holding the large model for queries an online classifier marked as hard.
Built the offline evaluation harness the team now gates releases on, 9,400 labelled cases across 6 task families, which caught 3 regressions that manual review had already passed.

Led the migration of 14 services onto a shared, versioned prompt schema, ending a class of production incidents caused by silent template drift, and mentored 4 engineers through their first on call rotation.
Shipped the vector search path serving 12k queries per second at p99 under 80ms, designing the sharding scheme that let the index grow 6x without a rewrite.

Diagnosed a recall collapse that three teams had attributed to the model, and traced it to a tokenizer version skew between indexing and serving; added the version assertion that makes the failure impossible.

Halved index build time, 9 hours to 4, by moving embedding generation to a batched GPU pipeline with checkpointing, and rewrote the query understanding service in Go for a 64% cut in p99 CPU time per request.

projects.name: tinyeval
bullets: An evaluation harness for retrieval systems that reports recall, latency and cost as one number per configuration, used by 40 teams inside two companies.
Runs the whole suite on CPU in under 3 minutes, because an evaluation nobody waits for is an evaluation nobody runs.

projects.name: shardlab
bullets: A simulator for vector index sharding strategies that predicts p99 latency within 8% of measured production, so a resharding decision can be argued from data rather than intuition.

skills.items: PyTorch, retrieval augmented generation, distillation, offline and online evaluation
AWS, Kubernetes, Terraform, Kafka, Postgres, Redis
Distributed systems design, performance profiling, incident response, observability

education.detail: Thesis on approximate nearest neighbour search under memory constraints.

cover_letter.subject: Application for Senior Machine Learning Engineer, REQ-4821
paragraphs: I am applying for the Senior Machine Learning Engineer role. I build retrieval and inference systems, most recently a two stage retriever that took median answer latency on a 40M document assistant from 2.4 seconds to 610 milliseconds, and I would like to do that work on Meridian's document intelligence platform.

The problem closest to yours is the one I spent last year on. Our assistant was accurate and too slow to use, and every proposal on the table was a bigger model or a bigger cache. The actual cost was re-ranking every query against the full candidate set. Splitting retrieval into a cheap recall stage and a cached precision stage cut latency by three quarters and, because the second stage ran far less often, cut inference spend 38% at the same time. Your posting describes a latency budget that will not move and a corpus that keeps growing, which is the same shape.

I also care about the part that is harder to demonstrate in an interview. Before any of that shipped, I built the evaluation harness the team now gates releases on: 9,400 labelled cases across six task families. It caught three regressions that manual review had passed. I would rather ship slowly against a measurement I trust than quickly against a demo.
I would welcome the chance to talk about how you are evaluating retrieval quality today, and where the latency budget is being spent. Thank you for your time.
